prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form that made incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part on B008 with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange confirmed that the dispute is about attribution and framing, not merit or maturity. Holst showed in humans that GLP-1 is a glucose-dependent incretin, Mojsov identified the biologically active truncated peptide, and Drucker defined proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor actions. That chain explains why the drugs work, and it has been confirmed in large independent outcome trials for glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal disease. A prize for physiology or medicine should anchor on the discovery step that made the therapy conceivable. The citation can still name the therapeutic consequence, as mine does, without crediting the analogue engineering. I also accept Sandberg's point that the case should rest on established outcomes. I therefore drop any weight on neurological benefit, which is still emerging.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains the four-names-for-three-slots problem. Knudsen's long-acting analogues, liraglutide and then semaglutide, are the form in which patients receive the physiology, and a basic-discovery trio can be read as leaving the drug unrecognised. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide against Habener and colleagues, who are not on the credited list, cannot be resolved from the supplied material, and that is the weakest point in my trio. A single large part also leaves out equally mature and cleanly documented work such as CAR-T, SMA antisense therapy and HPV vaccination. I have looked for a way to open a second part and I have not found one. The three-person ceiling would force a cut in B008's core, and each second-part candidate has its own unresolved credit problem.

responses.point: She proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation covering both the physiology and the development of protracted-action analogues, because a prize that stops at the physiology stops before the part that reached patients.
responses.response: This is the strongest alternative to my trio and I have weighed it again. Knudsen's contribution is real, and I accept that the committee has recognised arcs from mechanism to medicine. I still keep Mojsov for two reasons. A prize for discovery should credit the step that identified the active molecule, and without it the later analogue design had no defined target peptide. Also, a citation that reaches the drugs invites the question why other industrial contributors to long-acting design are not credited, and a three-person limit cannot answer that. My position is conditional, as it was in round 1. If the committee concludes that Mojsov's priority over Habener cannot be defended, I would support Knudsen in the third slot with the citation widened to cover the development of therapies. I would not move on the argument that the drug is what changed practice, because that argument would apply to any trio.

responses.point: He agrees that Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the most defensible trio, but says emerging neurological benefit should not count in the case, which should rest on established glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes.
responses.response: I accept the correction and I have changed my position on it. My round-1 remark about the gut-brain axis and appetite circuits was context, but the case does not need it and it is not established as a clinical benefit. I have taken it out of my case for this round. The established outcome evidence is enough, and my citation does not mention neurological effects. This changes the reasoning and not the configuration.

responses.point: He prefers June and Sadelain to any larger CAR-T set, because Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer and TIL work is a distinct line and Eshhar's originating chimeric receptor concept would remain unaddressed. For that reason he keeps B017 as an alternative and not as a second part.
responses.response: I agree on both points. Adding Rosenberg to a CAR-T prize widens it into adoptive cell transfer, and the third slot would be filled only because it is available. If B017 were taken up, I would prefer June and Sadelain, and I would want the committee to have a clear answer on Eshhar's concept first. I do not claim to have that answer from the supplied material. That is why I keep B017 as my first alternative and do not propose it as a second part. Your argument also settles my chair's question on a second part for me. With three people in total and B008 needing all three, a CAR-T part is not available unless B008's core is cut.

responses.point: He keeps optogenetics (B034) as the leading alternative if B008 stalled, and argues that channelrhodopsin was the discovery of a light-gated channel and not only a tool.
responses.response: I accept that channelrhodopsin is a discovery and not merely an invention, and I withdraw any suggestion that B034 is only a methods prize. It still fails on attribution. Neither of us has stated a principle that separates Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck from Hegemann, Nagel and Deisseroth, and a cut without a principle would be arbitrary. The clinical consequence is still early. I will not list it among my alternatives this round. B017 and B001 are mature and have a smaller attribution gap, and B034 remains a candidate for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide can be defended against Habener and colleagues. I cannot verify this from the supplied files and I treat it as the main risk to my configuration.

Whether the committee wants B008 framed as physiology or as the arc to therapies. That determines whether Mojsov or Knudsen holds the third slot, and I would not block Knudsen if the committee reaches the second view.
Whether a second prize part is feasible at all under the three-person ceiling, and whether B017 without Eshhar's concept, or B001 as a single-disease platform, would be defensible.
How much weight a prize citation should give to emerging neurological benefit of GLP-1 therapies. I give it none for now.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann on dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, and a postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard. None of the shortlisted achievements or credited names involves that work. I have not been shown any documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen or the other credited names. B030 (deep brain stimulation) is in my clinical field and is not on the shortlist. I do not see a need for recusal, and I have no update to the round-1 disclosure.
